To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the latent copying approach is able to achieve substantial improvements over existing approaches to question generation, and that the choice of reward function is a crucial factor in training a model to generate high-quality text.
(a) the generation path should be allowed to become latent, (b) policy gradient methods do not work well for this task and (c) the model will exploit weaknesses in the reward source.
the choice of generation mechanism should be latent and that reward functions should be aligned with human judgement.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of whether it is possible to generate high quality questions using reinforcement learning and a reward signal derived from human judgements.

the following questions: 1) Can a latent copying mechanism improve question generation? 2) Can a policy gradient method be used to optimise a reward source directly, or is the reward source poorly aligned with the human evaluation metric?
the following questions: How can we improve question generation? Is there a reward function that can improve the quality of the output? How can we learn a reward function from the ground truth?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
we are not sure how to build a model that is able to learn to generate questions, and that we need to be careful when designing training signals for this task.
we are not yet close to solving the question generation problem.

the most promising direction for question generation research is the use of adversarial training, but that the most promising approach for adversarial training is to use a latent copying mechanism to decouple the training objective from the ground truth, and to optimise for the reward signal directly.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
although there is still room for improvement, we are now in a position to make better informed decisions about the choice of objective and model architecture.
the current state of the art for Question Generation is not yet at a level that can be used in a real application, and that the current evaluation metrics are not aligned with human judgement.

we show that a model that is allowed to learn a latent generation path can achieve better performance on question generation than one that is biased to a single path, and that the model can be optimised for a quality objective that is better aligned with human judgement.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the choice of reward function is crucial to the success of reinforcement learning approaches, and that it is not always obvious which reward is best.

the choice of objective is crucial for the success of a model, but that there is a significant gap between the objectives used in previous approaches, and those which are aligned with human judgement.
although the task of question generation is similar to other sequence transformation problems, it requires a different approach to modelling and learning.
